PRODUCT REQUIREMENTS DOCUMENT
Fashion discovery and creator commerce, built for Nepal.

This document explains every screen in the product, what each button does, and where each link goes. It is written in plain English so that designers, developers, and non-technical team members can all use it.

Covers: web app, version 1 scope

2. What Outfiqe is
Outfiqe is a place to find clothes from Nepali brands.

Today, Nepali fashion is spread across many places. Some brands sell on Instagram. Some sell on TikTok. Some have a website. Many have nothing at all. A shopper who wants a new outfit has to search in five apps and still may not find anything good.

Outfiqe puts all of it in one place. But it is not just a shop. It is a guide. We show full outfits, not just single items. We show real people wearing the clothes, not only studio photos. And we only carry brands we have checked ourselves.

Three groups of people use the product. Each one needs something different.
Group
What they want

Shoppers
Clothes that suit their style, body, and budget — without hours of scrolling.

Brands

One person can be more than one of these. A creator also shops. A brand owner also buys clothes. Our account system is built for this, and we explain it in section 10.
4. How we will launch
The problem we have to solve first
Outfiqe needs three groups at once. But each group only joins if the others are already there:
A shopper will not visit an empty shop.
A brand will not upload products if nobody is shopping.
A creator will not post if nobody is watching.
If we build all three at the same time and open the doors, everything will be empty on day one. This is the single biggest risk to the project.
Our answer: do the first part by hand
We will not wait for brands to sign up. We will go and get them.
We personally contact 15 to 30 Nepali brands and ask them to join.
We collect their photos and prices over WhatsApp. No upload tool needed.
We build their brand page and their first outfits ourselves.
We launch to shoppers with a small but good catalogue.
Once shoppers are visiting, we invite creators, because now there is something to post about and someone to see it.
This manual work is not a shortcut we are ashamed of. It is the product. It is what makes the catalogue feel chosen rather than dumped.

Brand orange on white gives a contrast ratio of 3.3 to 1. Accessibility rules ask for 4.5 to 1 for normal text. So:

9.3 Product page
What it is for: to answer the two questions that stop people buying — can I trust this, and will it fit me.
Figure 5 — The product page. The "Worn by 5 creators" line sits between the price and the size choice.
The page has two zones
Zone 1 is controlled by the brand. These are the official product photos, the correct colour, shot in good light. This is what the buyer is actually buying.
Zone 2 is controlled by creators. These are real photos of real people wearing the item. They answer a different question, and they are more convincing.
These two zones must never be mixed. A creator may have styled the item differently or shot it in a different light. If the two are mixed, the buyer no longer knows which photo is the truth.
Figure 6 — The "Seen on creators" section, showing each creator height and the size they wear.
The trust line
Under the price sits a small row: three overlapping creator faces and the words "Worn by 5 creators". This is the single most important element on the page.
It works like a review count. The buyer does not want to read five posts. They want a half-second signal that other people trusted this. The number does that on its own.
Rules for the trust line
Rule
Reason
Hide it completely when the count is zero.
"Worn by 0 creators" is worse than showing nothing. It suggests nobody wanted the item.
Count creators, not posts.
One creator posting five times is still one person. Counting posts can be gamed.
Only count approved creators.
Otherwise anyone can turn on creator mode and inflate the number.
Show three faces, then the number.
More than three faces becomes visual mush at that size.
Store the count on the product.
The product grid shows this line on every card. Counting rows on each page load will be slow.
Height and size: the most valuable detail
Each creator photo shows their height and the size they are wearing, for example: 5 feet 4 inches, wearing S.

Almost nobody returns clothes because the photo was bad. They return them because the fit was wrong. A brand model photo can never answer "will this fit my body". Three creators of different heights, each with their size shown, answers it in one second. Height and size worn must be required fields on a tagged post.

What it is for: to show which brands are doing well, and to give shoppers a reason to come back each week.
Figure 9 — The brand leaderboard, showing rank and weekly movement.
Public or private?
The leaderboard is public. It is free advertising for brands who do well, and it helps a shopper trust a name they have never heard of.
But there is an important limit. Positions are public. Sales numbers are not.

If we publish "214 sold" next to a brand name, we are telling every competitor exactly what that brand earns. No brand will thank us for that. The public page shows rank, category, and whether the brand moved up or down. The brand sees its own real numbers inside its own dashboard, and nowhere else.
Rules
Split by category, so more brands can lead something.
Show only the top five or ten. Being unranked is neutral. Being publicly last is not, and a small brand may leave over it.
Do not launch this until there are roughly eight to ten brands in a category. Three names in a list makes the whole product look small.
Resets every Monday. The date range must be shown on the page.

Delivery address
Field
Notes
Full name
Prefilled from the account.
Phone
Required. This is how the rider reaches them, and it is the field COD depends on.

Free text. Tole, ward, and a landmark. We do not ask for a postcode; Nepal does not use them in practice.

Delivery is free over Rs. 5,000 and Rs. 150 below that. Inside the Kathmandu valley we promise two to three days. Outside it, four to seven.
Payment method

Three options, in this order. The order is deliberate: cash on delivery is first because it is what most Nepali shoppers still expect, and putting a wallet first would cost us orders from people who do not have one.
Method
When money moves
Why we offer it
Cash on delivery
When the rider hands the parcel over
The default. Removes all trust risk for a shopper who has never heard of us. Carries a Rs. 50 handling fee.
eSewa
Before the order is confirmed
The most used wallet in Nepal. Money is in hand before we ship, so there is no failed-delivery loss.
Khalti
Before the order is confirmed
Second wallet. Same flow as eSewa, different provider.

Only one method can be chosen. Choosing a wallet changes the button from "Place order" to "Pay Rs. 6,850", so the user knows money is about to move. Choosing cash on delivery adds the handling fee to the summary immediately, before they commit, never as a surprise at the end.
Why cash on delivery carries a fee

Cash on delivery costs us real money: the rider has to collect and reconcile cash, and a share of orders are refused at the door. The fee is small enough not to stop anyone using it, and large enough to nudge people towards paying up front once they trust us. We show the fee on the method itself, not in fine print.

10. Payment

This section covers what happens after the user presses the pay button. It is written against eSewa, because that is what we are integrating first. Khalti works the same way with different names, and the code should treat both as one interface with two implementations.
10.1 The eSewa flow, step by step
Step
What happens
1. User presses Pay
We create an Order in our database with payment status "initiated" and fulfilment status "draft". Nothing is visible to the brand yet.
2. We build a signed request
Amount, our merchant code, and a transaction reference we generate ourselves. The signature is made on our server with our secret key. It never touches the browser.
3. Hand over to eSewa
The browser is sent to eSewa. The user sees an eSewa screen, not ours. We show a short "Redirecting to eSewa" state first so the jump does not feel like a crash.
4. User approves in eSewa
They log in and confirm. We have no visibility into this step and must not pretend otherwise.
5. eSewa sends them back
To our success URL or our failure URL, with a reference.
6. We verify on the server
We call eSewa's status endpoint and check the amount and reference against the order we created in step 1.
7. We settle the order
On a verified match: payment status becomes "paid", fulfilment becomes "placed", stock is decremented, the brand is notified. Otherwise the order stays unpaid and we show the failure screen.
The rule that matters most

An order is only paid when our own server has verified it with eSewa. Landing on the success URL is not proof of anything: it is a URL, and anyone can visit it. Every payment must be confirmed server to server before we mark it paid or reduce stock.
Things that will go wrong, and what we do
Case
What we do
User closes the tab mid-payment
The order stays "initiated". A scheduled job re-checks it against eSewa for the next hour, then expires it. Stock is never held during this window.
eSewa says paid, we never got the redirect
The same re-check job finds it and settles the order. The user gets an email. This is why we poll rather than trusting the redirect alone.
Payment succeeds but the item sold out in between
We accept the payment, mark the order for refund, and contact the buyer the same day. We do not silently cancel. This is why stock is decremented at verification and not before.
The same payment is submitted twice
Our transaction reference is unique per order and we reject a second settlement against it. Every write must be safe to run twice.
Amount does not match
Never settle. Log it, alert us, and show the failure screen. A mismatch is either a bug or an attack.
10.2 What we never store
We never see or store an eSewa PIN, password, or wallet balance. That exchange happens on eSewa's own screens.
We store the transaction reference, the amount, the method, and the time. Nothing else about the payment.
Our secret key lives on the server only, in environment configuration. It is never sent to the browser and never committed to the repository.
10.3 Refunds in version 1

There is no refund button. Refunds are done by hand, by us, through the eSewa merchant dashboard, and then recorded against the order. Automating refunds before we have volume would be effort spent on a path almost nobody takes.
11. Orders and inventory
11.1 The two statuses

An order has two separate statuses, and confusing them is the most common mistake in this kind of system. A cash-on-delivery order is unpaid but perfectly valid and should be packed and shipped. A prepaid order is paid on the day it is placed and still has days of delivery ahead of it.
Status
Values
Meaning
Payment
initiated, paid, due, failed, refunded
"Due" is a cash-on-delivery order that is not yet collected. It is a normal, healthy state, not an error.
Fulfilment
placed, packed, shipped, delivered, cancelled
Where the parcel physically is. Drives the tracker the shopper sees.
The shopper sees both, as two small badges on the order row. Hiding the payment status would leave a cash-on-delivery buyer unsure whether they still owe money.
11.2 Your orders
What it is for: to answer "where is my parcel" without the shopper having to message us.
Element
What it does
Order row
Order number, first product photo, date, method, total, and the two status badges. Tapping expands it.
Tracker
Four dots: Order placed, Packed, On the way, Delivered. Dots up to the current status are filled orange.
Payment line
The method and, for wallet orders, the transaction reference. For cash on delivery it reads "collect on delivery".
Item lines
Every product with its size, quantity, and price, so the total can be checked.
Empty state
When there are no orders, an invitation to shop. When signed out, a sign-in prompt.
11.3 Stock rules
Rule
Why
Stock is held per product and per size, never per product alone
Selling the last medium is not the same as selling out. A single number would oversell every popular size.
A size with zero stock is shown, struck through, and not selectable
Removing it entirely makes the shopper think we never carried their size. Showing it sold out is honest and tells them to check back.
Stock is decremented when payment is verified, or when a cash-on-delivery order is placed
Not when an item is added to a bag. Holding stock for abandoned bags would make a small catalogue look empty.
Nothing is reserved while a payment is in progress
Simpler, and at our volume the collision is rare. Section 10 explains how we handle it when it does happen.
Cancelled or refunded orders return their stock
Otherwise the catalogue quietly shrinks every time something goes wrong.
11.4 Who does what after an order
Step
Who
How, in version 1
Order comes in
Us
We are emailed, and it appears in the brand dashboard.
Brand is told
Us
By hand, over WhatsApp, the same way we onboard them. No brand-side tooling yet.
Parcel is packed
Brand
They mark it packed in the dashboard, or tell us and we do it.
Delivery
Courier
A local courier. We update the status; there is no live tracking integration in version 1.
Cash is collected
Courier
Settled with us weekly. We then pay the brand, minus our cut.

All of this is deliberately manual. At ten orders a day a person can do it in twenty minutes, and doing it by hand teaches us what to automate. We should not build brand-side order tooling until a brand asks for it twice.
12. Accounts and roles
One account, different modes
We do not build separate account types for shoppers, creators, and brand owners. One person can be all three. Splitting them means two logins, two password resets, and a painful merge later.
Instead there is one account, and switches on top of it.
Figure 17 — The profile menu with creator mode switched on. Three extra items appear.
Creator mode
Any signed-in user can turn on creator mode from the profile menu. Turning it on changes four things:
A "Create a post" action appears.
Their profile gains a posts grid and a follower count.
The post composer gains the product tagging step.
If they are approved, an earnings section appears.

Nothing else changes. Same bag, same saved items, same orders. A creator is still a shopper. This matters, because a creator posting about something they actually bought is far more convincing than one posting about a free gift.
Posting is open. Earning is not.
This is an important split.
Setting
Who controls it
What it means
Creator mode on or off
The user
They can post and tag products.
Approved creator
Outfiqe
They can earn commission, and they count towards "worn by X creators".

If anyone could earn money the moment they switched a toggle, people would spam tagged links for clothes they have never worn. That destroys the credibility of the whole feed, which is the only reason it works.
Brand accounts
A brand is not a user type either. It is a link between a user and a brand.
The brand applies through the public form. No account exists yet.
We review, and if it is a fit, we approve.
The system creates a single-use invite link and sends it by email or WhatsApp.
They open the link and set a password. The account is created and connected to the brand.
They land in the dashboard.
Because the link between user and brand is stored separately, a brand can add staff later without any change to the database.
Invite links must be stored as a hash, never as plain text. If the database leaks, plain invite links are account takeover.
13. Creator tagging and who gets paid
How a sale is linked to a creator
A shopper sees a creator post and taps the tagged product.
We record the click: which post, which product, which visitor.
The shopper lands on the normal product page.
They add to bag and check out.
The order stores which post sent them.
The sale always happens on our product page, never inside the post. We do not copy prices or stock into posts, because those change and the post would show old information.
Two rules we must publish
How long does credit last?
Seven days. If a shopper taps a post today and buys nine days later, the creator does not earn. Pick a number and publish it, so creators are not guessing.
What if several creators posted the same item?
The last post the buyer tapped wins.

An alternative is to split the commission between everyone. Do not do this. It sounds fairer, but it produces tiny unpredictable payments, and a creator cannot tell whether posting is worth their time. Predictable beats fair here.
Write this sentence on the creator terms page before launch:
"Credit goes to the last post you clicked before buying, within 7 days. If you clicked several creators’ posts, the most recent one earns the commission."
The first argument about this will happen within weeks of switching payouts on. Having that sentence already published turns a fight into a link.
Other payment rules
Rule
Reason
A creator cannot earn commission on their own purchase.
Otherwise they tag an item, click their own link, and give themselves a discount. Because we use one account per person, we can actually check this.
Credit is given per item, not per order.
If someone buys three things and only one came from a post, only that item pays commission.
If no post was clicked, no creator is paid.
The sale was organic. We keep the full margin. Attribution must default to nobody.
Payouts wait until the return window closes.
So we do not pay commission on an order that comes back.
Show every creator their own clicks, even on sales they lost.
A creator who sees "312 clicks, 4 sales" understands the system. One who only sees payouts assumes it is rigged.

15. Empty, loading, and error states
These are not edge cases. On a new product they are what most people will see first.
Situation
What we show
Page is loading
Grey placeholder shapes in the same layout as the real content, so nothing jumps when it arrives.
A style or category has no products
A short message and a link to something that does have products. Never a blank grid.
Product has no creator posts
Hide the trust line and the whole "Seen on" section. Do not show a zero.
Saved list, signed out
Explain that saves live with the account, and offer a Sign in button.
Bag is empty
An invitation to start shopping, with a button.
Payment is being verified
A short "Redirecting to eSewa" state. Never a blank screen, and never a button they can press twice.
Payment failed or was cancelled
Explain plainly, keep the bag exactly as it was, and offer to try again or switch method. Never lose the bag.
No orders yet
An invitation to shop. Signed out, a sign-in prompt instead.
No personalised feed yet
Show popular or hand-picked content instead. Never an empty feed.
A photo fails to load
A plain grey block of the correct shape. Never a broken image icon.
Hero fails to load
Keep the top bar and everything below. The page must still work.
16. Measuring success
Three numbers matter most in the first months. Together they tell us which problem we have.
Number
What it tells us
Outfit and product views
Are people arriving at all?
Saves per visitor
Is our selection any good? If people browse but never save, our curation is wrong.
Click-through to a product from a post
Is the creator layer working?
Also track: hero clicks, style card choices, category choices, add to bag rate, search usage, likes and comments, leaderboard taps, and how many people use Explore instead of Shop.
17. Quality requirements
Speed
The top bar, hero, and first row of products must appear quickly. Everything else can arrive after.
Images must be sized for the screen they are shown on. Most of our traffic will be on phones with slow connections.
Works on phones
The product grid goes from five across on a computer, to four, to three, to two on a phone.
The Explore feed goes from three columns to two to one.
Test every screen at 360 pixels wide before calling it done. That is where most Nepali traffic will be.
Accessibility
Every button must be reachable and visible when using a keyboard.
Icon-only buttons need a text label for screen readers.
Orange text on white must use the deep orange, not the brand orange. See section 6.
If a person has asked their device to reduce motion, the hero must stop moving on its own.
Built to be changed
Styles, categories, collections, and leaderboard types come from the database, not from the code.
Product cards, creator post cards, category pills, and the trust line are each one component, used everywhere.
18. Decisions still open
These need an answer before the work starts. Each one changes the build.
Question
Our current thinking
How does a shopper actually pay? (decided)
Decided: we take the order in-app. Cash on delivery is the default, with eSewa and Khalti for anyone who prefers to pay up front. We still pass the order to the brand by hand. See sections 10 and 11.
Does the Shop and Explore toggle change the whole site or just the home page?
Just the home page in version 1.
Does the top bar stay stuck while scrolling?
Yes, on all screens.
Do product grids use pages, a View all button, or endless scrolling?
View all in version 1. Simplest to build.
Do we give creators a discount on their own purchases?
Probably yes. It is cleaner than letting them earn commission on themselves.
Who supplies product photography?
Unresolved, and this is a real risk. The design assumes photos of a consistent quality. Collecting them over WhatsApp will not give us that.
Do we launch the leaderboard at the same time as everything else?
No. Wait until there are enough brands per category.
19. When is version 1 finished?
Version 1 is finished when all of the following are true.
A first-time visitor understands what Outfiqe is without anyone explaining it.
Everything except saving, following, and buying works without an account.
A shopper can find clothes by style and by clothing type.
Every product card shows the brand, the name, the price, and the creator count when there is one.
A product with no creator posts hides the trust line completely.
Tapping a tagged product in a post opens the right product page and records which post sent them.
Signing in from the middle of an action finishes that action afterwards.
Creator mode can be turned on and off, and changes only what it should.
A brand can apply, be approved, receive an invite, sign in, and add products.
Products stay in review until we approve them.
Every screen works at 360 pixels wide.
Every screen has a proper empty state.
A sold-out size cannot be selected or added to the bag.
A shopper can complete an order with cash on delivery, and with eSewa.
An order is only marked paid after our server has verified it with eSewa.
Stock goes down when the order settles, and not when something is added to a bag.
Payment status and delivery status are shown separately, and a cash-on-delivery order reads as due rather than as an error.
Closing the tab mid-payment never leaves an order stuck as paid or as lost.
